We bound the value of this game above and below in terms of a combinatorial online learning quantity: the sequential fat-shattering dimension, which we characterize for the $\ell_p / \ell_q$ case. Our results generally apply when the feasible set $\mathcal{X}$ and the set of possible subgradients $\mathcal{H}$ admit a type of minimax theorem, advancing on a fundamental question by Sridharan (Sri12, Section 10.1.2, Q3). As a geometric consequence of our analysis, of independent interest, we obtain estimates for the expected distance of a convex hull of samples to their mean in several Banach geometries, a version of the celebrated Wendel's theorem (Wen62), but quantitative and for bounded general distributions as opposed to centrally symmetric ones.
item.dc:creator: Brian Bullins, Crist\'obal Guzm\'an, David Mart\'inez-Rubio, Mathieu Molina

item.title: Stable Movement for Nondual Lipschitz Convex Optimization: Efficiency and Nearly Optimal Oracle Rates
item.description: arXiv:2609.20701v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study efficient algorithms for realizing the first-order oracle complexity of optimization of $G$-Lipschitz convex functions with respect to the $\ell_q$-norm over an $\ell_p$-ball of radius $R$, where $1\leq p,q\leq\infty$. For $p<q$, we obtain error $\widetilde{O}_{p,q}(GR/T^{1/p-(1/q-1/2)_{+}})$ after $T$ oracle queries, attaining the lower bounds in a COLT 2015 open problem (Guz15b) with efficient algorithms. In particular, the rate is $\widetilde{O}(GR/T)$ for Euclidean Lipschitzness with an $\ell_1$-ball domain of radius $R$ ($p=1,q=2$). Our solution consists of reducing convex Lipschitz optimization to the chasing nested convex sets problem (BBE+20) in sublevel sets of an evolving maximum of affine lower bounds, that is, the bundle (LNN95): at each query we either find a point with low function value or we produce a deep cut in the current sublevel of the bundle that we chase. The dichotomy between stability of selectors and forced movement by deep cuts bounds the number of iterations of the algorithm nearly optimally. For nested convex subsets of the $\ell_p$ ball $R B_p^d$, we introduce novel stable selectors whose movement is nearly optimal in high dimensions. A Monte Carlo average of the proposed selector achieves near-optimal rates with high probability and can be implemented for our optimization algorithm in polynomial time in the real-arithmetic model.
item.dc:creator: David Mart\'inez-Rubio, Crist\'obal Guzm\'an

item.title: Forecasting Brain Tracer Distribution from Pre-Contrast MRI: A Comparison of Direct Regression and Flow Matching
item.description: arXiv:2609.22377v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The brain fluid clearance system can be studied with intrathecal contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). By injecting a tracer into the spinal canal and performing MRI over 24--48\,h, one can measure how a tracer injected into the cerebrospinal fluid spreads through the brain. As this is an invasive procedure requiring several MRI scans, we ask how much of the later tracer distribution can be predicted from the pre-contrast scan and elapsed time alone. Using 104 training patients (878 MRI volumes), we compared a direct image-to-image regression model with a more complex generative model based on conditional flow matching, and tested both on 23 held-out patients and on 51 patients from a separate cohort with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH). Relative to simply copying the pre-contrast scan, the direct model reduced the mean absolute error (intensities normalized to $[0,1]$) from 0.089 to 0.036, about 60\%, in held-out patients and from 0.075 to 0.056, about 25\%, in the iNPH cohort. The reduction held in every sampled elapsed-time interval and brain compartment, and errors remained largest at 20--30\,h and in the ventricles, where enhancement is strongest. Its predicted change maps agreed with the observed tracer enhancement rather than only reproducing anatomy. The generative model was less accurate in both cohorts. A substantial part of the later tracer distribution is therefore predictable from the patient's brain anatomy as seen on pre-contrast MRI, and the added model complexity gave no benefit at this data scale. Whether this accuracy suffices for a given clinical use remains to be established; with prospective validation, such forecasts could help simplify the MRI protocol used to assess brain clearance.
item.dc:creator: Qinghui Liu, Jon Andr\'e Ottesen, Thu Nguyen, Geir Ringstad, Ingrid Mossige, Siri Fl{\o}gstad Svensson, Sissel Riis Kalstad, Atle Bj{\o}rnerud, Per Kristian Eide, Kyrre Eeg Emblem

item.title: When Pass@$k$ Crossovers Are Real - and Why: Paired Inference and the Markov Kernel of RLVR
item.description: arXiv:2609.22547v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically improves pass@1 but can fall behind its base model at large sampling budgets $k$, commonly interpreted as sharpening existing solutions. Because adjacent pass@$k$ estimates reuse generations, pointwise error bars cannot establish a crossover. We formulate paired inference on the RL-minus-base difference curve: a prompt-level multiplier bootstrap yields a one-sided dominance test and simultaneous confidence bands requiring both an early gain and a later loss. Among nine public RLVR checkpoints at 3k-16k token limits, only one narrowly meets this criterion before multiplicity adjustment; asymmetric truncation can create, mask, or reverse crossovers. On 1,060 deduplicated competition problems at 32k tokens, two 1.5B models exhibit certified crossovers around $k\approx10$-$60$, while two 7B models show no supported loss. A paired variance decomposition shows why adding prompts improves power more than deeper sampling. Prompts with identical base success probability diverge after RLVR, with dispersion replicating across independent generation halves and violating Lipschitz slope bounds for reasonable deterministic maps. Modeling RLVR as a Markov kernel, Jensen's inequality shows that conditional dispersion depresses pass@$k$ for $k\ge2$. Once dispersion is modeled, the conditional-mean log-odds slope is below one in every pair: RLVR improves hard prompts on average, while late-$k$ loss comes from a 2%-3% minority of base-solved prompts collapsing onto a repeated modal wrong answer and resisting prefix rescue up to 4,096 tokens. In controlled runs from one base model on 3,000 new problems, all four GRPO arms fall behind near $k\approx200$ and remain behind through $k=4096$, while SFT stays significantly ahead throughout.
item.dc:creator: Chen Yang

item.title: Agentic Detection of Online Conspiracies
item.description: arXiv:2609.30250v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conspiratorial discourse on social media is not always expressed through explicit claims or stable lexical markers. The same surface content may express endorsement, legitimate concerns, criticism, satire, or mockery. The main challenge is therefore not only recognizing conspiracy-related claims, but inferring the speaker's intent -- the utterance's illocutionary force. We argue that this can be achieved through the use of relevant social contexts and propose an agentic framework, equipped with a set of tools supporting social queries. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach on a unique dataset of Hebrew tweets, covering 80%--90% of the public Hebrew tweets published over a four-year span (late 2018-- early 2023), encompassing several election cycles as well as the COVID pandemic years and related vaccination campaigns. This extensive coverage can be used in recovering different social contexts. Evaluating our framework on a manually-annotated adversarial dataset, we find that context-aware workflows consistently outperform text-only classification and that the agentic framework performs better than other frameworks and settings, with significant gains over a non-agentic model exposed to the same contexts available to the agent. We further provide an analysis of the results, the errors and efficiency (token economy) tradeoffs. These findings support viewing the task of conspiracy detection as a socially embedded interpretation task, in which effective classification depends not only on access to contexts, but also on adaptive reasoning in which the agent uses tools on a per-case basis, asking only for evidence relevant to its current reasoning step.
item.dc:creator: Lior Biton, Oren Tsur

item.title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.10942v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.
item.dc:creator: Daksh Raghuvanshi, Ved Vedere, Yifan Wang

item.title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
item.description: arXiv:2610.14423v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.
item.dc:creator: Aditi Khandelwal, Ayush K. Tarun, Yixuan Xu, Imanol Schlag, Golnoosh Farnadi, Siva Reddy, Luke Zettlemoyer, Antoine Bosselut

item.title: ToPA: Block-wise Toeplitz Adaptation for Expressive and Efficient Fine-Tuning
item.description: arXiv:2610.22883v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has emerged as a prevalent strategy for adapting large pre-trained models. Among PEFT techniques, reparameterization-based methods, particularly those that employ low-rank or sparsity structures, have attracted significant attention. However, these approaches often underperform full fine-tuning. Specifically, low-rank methods constrain the update rank, which is misaligned with the inherently high-rank nature of full fine-tuning. In contrast, sparsity-based techniques limit the flexibility of the parameter space and compromise connectivity across weights. To overcome these limitations, we explore the use of Toeplitz matrices, whose entries are constant along each diagonal, therefore providing a compact parameterization without imposing explicit rank or sparsity constraints. A straightforward approach is to update weights via a product of Toeplitz matrices. However, similar to RNNs, long multiplicative chains often lead to gradient instability. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{ToPA}, a more refined version of this idea that replaces standard Toeplitz matrices with block-wise Toeplitz, greatly increasing each factor's capacity and shortening the chain, thereby stabilizing training and improving expressiveness. We theoretically show that products of block-wise Toeplitz matrices can approximate arbitrary matrices under shorter chain length, justifying the structural design of ToPA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ToPA offers greater expressivity than existing low-rank and sparse parameterizations. Empirical evaluations across 21 NLP and CV datasets, spanning 5 model architectures, consistently validate the effectiveness of ToPA.
item.dc:creator: Sicong Li, Qianqian Xu, Zhiyong Yang, Zitai Wang, Longtao Huang, Xiaochun Cao, Qingming Huang

item.title: SPELUNKA: A Framework for Finding Unanticipated Associations in Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.23979v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are the backbone of many state-of-the-art multimodal systems, but often encode spurious and harmful associations from their training data. While prior work focuses on removing known biases from VLMs, methods for discovering unanticipated associations for retrieval tasks remain underexplored. We introduce SPELUNKA, an automated, inference-time framework for finding unanticipated distributional biases for retrieval tasks in VLMs without pre-specified labeled subgroups, inference-time human supervision, or model fine-tuning. Given a concept of interest, SPELUNKA generates captions for related images, extracts relevant entities from captions, and selects semantically meaningful associations. A frequency-based detection rule then identifies spurious associations by measuring over- or under-representation of these attributes in a VLM's top-ranked outputs relative to their full dataset distribution. We evaluate SPELUNKA across four datasets, and find that it 1) successfully recovers both synthetic and naturally occurring spurious correlations, 2) achieves an average AUROC of 0.93 across four datasets in identifying images strongly associated with a query, and 3) outperforms baselines in finding features that are strongly associated with a given query.
item.dc:creator: Cassandra Parent, Isha Agarwal, Kumail Alhamoud, Charikleia Moraitaki, Rafiya Javed, Walter Gerych, Marzyeh Ghassemi

item.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
item.description: arXiv:2610.24715v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so the probability that a loop survives $m$ more repetitions is, under any sampler, a product of per-step continuation probabilities computable from one forward pass. A lock, where this probability stays exactly one, is its limiting case. Pure sampling never locks; top-$p$ with threshold $\pi>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $\pi$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis shows a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $\lambda b^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 61% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 0.2% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 199 loops that survive DRY, on six models, have $g\le 7$. We propose a count term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window, and closes this blind spot. Added to DRY (DRY-C), it cuts loops in 1,800 structured generations on five models from 167 to 34, and loops reaching the length limit from 150 to 0, with reasoning accuracy and item coverage on par with DRY. DRY's own length term costs 2.5 to 14.2 points of accuracy on GSM8K and MATH-500; used in its place, the count term keeps the default sampler's accuracy and leaves one of the 1,800 generations at the limit.
item.dc:creator: Yichuan Chen, Xin Wang

item.title: Near Minimax Rates for Quantile Distributional Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.29595v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we study quantile distributional policy evaluation, where the return distribution under a given policy is approximated by the quantile Bellman fixed point $\bm\eta_m$. We investigate the statistical accuracy of estimating $\bm\eta_m$ across quantile resolutions under Wasserstein distances. Assuming access to a generative model, we construct a quantile fixed point estimator $\bm\eta_m^{(n)}$ from an empirical Markov decision process of $n$ observations per state-action pair and establish non-asymptotic error bounds under Wasserstein distances. When reward densities are uniformly bounded away from zero, we obtain a root-$n$ high-probability bound simultaneously over all resolutions $m$ and all Wasserstein orders $1\le p\le\infty$. When reward densities vanish at the support endpoints, we show that continuity and endpoint monotonicity suffice to preserve the same resolution-independent rate for $1\le p\le2$. For $p>2$, we establish a root-$n$ bound with coefficient $m^{1/2-1/p}$, together with a slower, resolution-independent $n^{-1/p}$ bound for every finite $p>2$. We further obtain resolution-independent $W_\infty$ consistency governed by the continuity modulus of reward quantile functions. To investigate the sharpness of these bounds, we characterize the exact local asymptotic minimax risk at each fixed resolution as the expected Wasserstein-coordinate norm of the efficient Gaussian limit and prove that our estimator attains it. We then examine the resolution dependence of this optimal local risk. A regular one-state instance has resolution-independent local risk constants, whereas a single endpoint-vanishing two-state instance exhibits growth of order $m^{1/2-1/p}$, up to logarithmic factors along a resolution subsequence, for every $p>2$.
item.dc:creator: Zijie Cheng, Zhihua Zhang

item.title: No Frames, Just Frequencies: Bandwidth-Efficient Deployment-Time Adaptation for Smart Glasses
item.description: arXiv:2610.29607v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep neural networks deployed on smart glasses must adapt to changes in the distribution of incoming data while adhering to strict privacy and device constraints. We present No Frames, Just Frequencies, a bandwidth-efficient source-assisted adaptation framework that characterizes distribution shifts using compact frequency descriptors computed on-device. Rather than transmitting camera frames, the glasses compute and send frequency descriptors to a host device that contains a replica of the model. The host device maps the received frequency descriptor to a distribution shift operator that synthesizes out-of-distribution data and adapts a model replica using a pre-defined adaptation protocol. We evaluate the framework on mixtures of ImageNet-C corruptions using convolution-based (ConvNeXtV2-Femto), self-attention-based (DeiT-Tiny), and hybrid (TinyViT-5M) vision models, on person classification (Visual Wake Words), and on object detection (MS-COCO). Our results reveal that adaptation driven solely by the transmitted descriptors recovers $93-95\%$ of the supervised oracle adaptation gain on all three architectures, $82\%$ on Visual Wake Words and $94$--$98\%$ on MS-COCO. Notably, adaptation quality degrades gracefully as the descriptor resolution decreases from $224 $ to $28$ pixels, consistently across architectures, enabling bandwidth reductions from $213\times$ to $784\times$ across the frequency descriptors.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Corti, Moritz Becker, Olga Saukh

item.title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization for Agentic Robotics
item.description: arXiv:2610.35817v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra now directly control robots and can generalize better than vision-language-action models (VLAs). We argue that this ability could arise from two distinct, composable skills: semantic reasoning, to understand what a task asks for in a scene, and motion control, to move the robot to do it. We show that small open VLMs are already capable of the first and mainly lack the second. We introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches this missing motion skill, entirely in simulation on simple primitive tasks and from the model's own successes, with no frontier teacher or distillation and no real-world robot data. ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper, and 74.0% on a bimanual adaptation of RoboLab-120, on par with GPT-6 Astra's 72.2%. ZAP also generalizes to new objects, goals, and strategies, and in simulation to a robot embodiment on which it never trained.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch, Thomas Neff

item.title: Dexterous In-Hand Object Pose Reaching with Learned Safety Filters
item.description: arXiv:2610.37652v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is the next frontier of robotics, yet learned hand skills remain limited to simple grasps or basic repeated motions, such as rotating an object. As robots attempt more demanding in-hand maneuvers, safety, such as not dropping the object, becomes critical, yet it is rarely measured. We study in-hand object pose reaching, a task that demands diverse and difficult grasps: moving an object to almost any position and orientation within reach of the fingers, at any wrist orientation, through long sequences of consecutive goals. We present a recipe for training such policies for a LEAP hand in simulation without human data, built on a range of insights, from diverse resets and goals via generated grasp datasets to an adaptive friction curriculum. With careful system identification, the policies transfer zero-shot to the real hand, using either motion capture or a single wrist-mounted depth camera, and prove remarkably capable and robust. On top of the task policy, we add a learned residual safety filter with adjustable conservativeness, letting us tune the balance between performance and safety and greatly reduce object drops. In 13.3 hours of real-robot evaluation over 4,800 unseen goals across 4 objects and diverse wrist orientations, the state-based policy reaches 95.2% of goals within 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and the filter cuts its drops by 75% while still reaching 91.5% of goals. The policies can also spin a lightbulb held in an arbitrary pose, reach out-of-distribution goals, withstand fast arm motion and perturbations, and, needing only a wrist camera, serve as portable skills such as screwing in a lightbulb. We release the full recipe as a platform for studying performance, reliability, and safety in high-dimensional dexterous systems. Videos and more are available at https://ian-chuang.github.io/dexsafe/.
item.dc:creator: Ian Chuang, Hiya Shah, Vamsi Chilamkur, Iman Soltani, Claire Tomlin

item.title: Opening the Box Changes the Cat: LLMs Detect Chain-of-Thought Monitoring - What now?
item.description: arXiv:2610.40946v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning allows large language models (LLMs) to generate intermediate reasoning traces in natural language while solving complex tasks. These traces can support safety monitoring by exposing potentially harmful plans before actions are executed. In this work, we investigate the conditions under which LLMs infer the presence of CoT monitoring from direct and indirect environmental cues and examine how this inference affects their subsequent behavior. Our observations suggest that oversight is an interactive process: while a monitor inspects a model's reasoning, traces left by monitoring interventions can allow the model to infer that its thoughts are being observed and to adapt its behavior accordingly. We show that even subtle environmental cues, such as timing-related signals from timeouts and operation durations, can reveal the presence of monitoring and trigger models to adapt their behavior to evade oversight. Across repeated episodes and interaction loops, we further observe that models can form statistical estimates of the monitor's effectiveness and use these estimates to guide attempts to evade detection. These findings highlight the need to evaluate CoT-based oversight under adaptive conditions, where the monitoring process itself may influence the behavior it seeks to observe.
item.dc:creator: Amir Jalilifard, Marcos Medeiros Raimundo, Anderson Rocha

item.title: SAT-ACT: Learning CDCL Branching from Outcome-Derived Action Preferences
item.description: arXiv:2610.41290v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning-based approaches have increasingly been explored for SAT solving, with particular attention to improving branching decisions in conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) solvers. These approaches derive branching guidance either from static structural properties of SAT formulas or from dynamic signals obtained through solver feedback and execution traces. However, these forms of supervision provide limited evidence about state-dependent branching effects, while different outcome measures may favor different branching choices. To address these limitations, we propose SAT-ACT, an outcome-derived learning framework for CDCL branching. We design three complementary outcome comparison criteria to extract action preferences from independent branching action rollouts initiated at the same solver state. The criteria identify preferences supported by the outcomes and leave comparisons unresolved when the evidence is insufficient or conflicting, instead of forcing an ordering using a predefined scalar metric. A state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from the extracted preferences and uses them to guide CDCL search directly without online action rollouts. We further introduce non-dominated heuristic action supervision, which retains the solver-selected action as a training target only when it remains non-dominated under these preferences. Solver-level experiments show that SAT-ACT consistently reduces CDCL search costs on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on the SAT Competition benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Zhenchao Sun, Chongyang Tao, Ping Lu, Tongkai Lu, Jianling Gao, Shuai Ma

item.title: Answer Correction with Verifiable Rewards: A Gemma-Family Study of Multi-View Driving QA
item.description: arXiv:2611.00828v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-camera driving question answering provides a discrete test of vision-language models, but post-training gains can reflect changed selected answers or improved answer extraction. We investigate this distinction within the Gemma model family using archived, task-linked WaymoQA evaluations. A zero-shot diagnostic on 5,519 test questions spans effective-small, mixture-of-experts, unified, and dense checkpoints, with serving differences disclosed rather than interpreted as architecture effects. The strongest controlled evidence is a matched-harness Gemma-4-12B base/GRPO pair: accuracy rises from 73.78% to 75.43%, a gain of 1.65 percentage points with a scene-cluster bootstrap interval of [+0.84, +2.41]. There are 215 improvements and 124 regressions; 213 improvements start from an extractable but incorrect base answer, and only two recover previously unextractable responses. Crossing correctness with extraction state shows why correct noncompliant outputs cannot be counted as prediction errors. Category counts reveal a critical safety asymmetry: routine perception gains (+5.93 pp) mask a regression in safety-critical hazard prediction (-1.82 pp), demonstrating that unweighted outcome rewards can trade off rare edge cases for aggregate accuracy. Reward saturation describes sampled training dynamics rather than an architectural ceiling. A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison yields no detected average improvement, with uncertainty that does not establish equivalence. These results support a modest answer-selection gain for the recorded tuning configuration and a reproducible diagnostic accounting, without attributing corrected labels to specific grounding mechanisms or claiming superiority over matched supervised tuning.
item.dc:creator: T N Rickesh, Pranav Vinodh, Sowmya Kamath S

item.title: Fewer Tokens, More Answers: Verifiable-Reward Tuning of an Ornith-Style VLM for Multi-View Driving QA
item.description: arXiv:2611.00833v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reasoning-enabled model derivatives must turn intermediate deliberation into a usable answer within a deployment budget. We study that transition in an Ornith checkpoint adapted to multi-camera driving question answering with verifiable rewards. Paired archived outputs show that, on a selected 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, GRPO increases answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%. Of 39 wrong-to-correct transitions, 33 begin with an unextractable base response. The base's 87 unextractable responses all reach the token cap. Checkpoint-verified reconstruction on those same questions gives a much smaller first-pass accuracy gain at 512 tokens: +0.75 percentage points, versus +8.25 at 256. A later answer-cued continuation is analyzed separately; it helps the base more and narrows the adapter difference. On the full 2,511-question development set, this recovery-enabled pipeline reduces mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain. We frame these findings as adaptation of answer delivery under finite budgets, with explicit selection and provenance limits. Ornith's self-scaffolding lineage and newer reasoning-enabled derivatives such as Bonsai motivate the problem, but our measured results concern Ornith alone and do not establish a shared architectural mechanism or cross-model transfer.
item.dc:creator: T N Rickesh, Pranav Vinodh, Sowmya Kamath S

item.title: How Close to the Theme? Similarity-Label Conditioning for Game Music Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.01047v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Composers develop music from an original idea, controlling how similar each new section is to it, from near repetition to new material. Game music needs this often, as its material repeats over long play. Music models, however, rarely learn to control similarity from real pieces. We further train a pretrained MIDI model on section pairs from Super Mario pieces. A label states each pair's similarity, and a context vector summarises the given section, or context. For 157 test contexts, the model generates six outputs per label. Twelve measures score the outputs; one main measure each covers melody, pitch content, rhythm and note length. On average, outputs requested as similar are more similar to their context than those requested as dissimilar, and not to other pieces. All twelve measures favour them; each main measure stays significant after correction for multiple tests. On melody, the gap comes mainly from more frequent restatement of the context's melody. Against an otherwise identical model without a label, only the request for high similarity makes outputs more similar. In a listening test, ratings followed melodic overlap with the context most closely of all measures.
item.dc:creator: Shangxuan Luo, Zixun Guo, Jinjie Shi, Joshua Reiss

item.title: Write Facts the Way Models Read Them: Lifting the Two-Hop Curse
item.description: arXiv:2611.01519v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A language model that learns a new fact by fine-tuning can repeat it but cannot reason with it: taught that a person is a citizen of a new country, it still cannot say, without chain-of-thought, who the head of state of that person's country is. This two-hop curse is widely treated as a reasoning deficit, and the strongest knowledge editors answer it with synthesized reasoning data. We show that the reasoning is intact and the writing is wrong. Fine-tuning writes a new fact as an answer to be said, whereas the second hop reads the bridge ("that person's country") as an entity, from the middle layers on: patching the model's own representation of the entity into the bridge at those layers largely restores the second hop, yet after fine-tuning the bridge there is no closer to the new entity than before the edit. We therefore propose read-equivalent writing (Legible): one loss term makes the bridge phrase, at the layer where the second hop finishes reading it, match the model's own reading of the new entity, and keeps the same relation's other subjects unchanged. Phrases and targets come from the edited model itself, and no multi-hop training data is used. Across Qwen2.5, Llama-3 and Qwen3, Legible (I) composes learned facts more often than the model composes its own knowledge, on MQuAKE's two-hop-curse questions; (II) reaches 1.8-2.6x the bridge accuracy of CaKE, whose reasoning data composes no better than plain fine-tuning, and has the best average over composition, accuracy and locality against four families of writers; and (III) lifts the curse on RippleEdits, on the benchmark of Balesni et al., who named the curse, and at 14B.
item.dc:creator: Zhiyun Shi

item.title: Seeing Why: Exact Evidence Maps for Quantum and Optical Image Classifiers
item.description: arXiv:2611.01993v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When an image classifier decides, we can usually only estimate why. For quantum and all-optical classifiers that act linearly on amplitude-encoded pictures up to the measurement, with no trained classical network before or after them, each class's Born probability above its no-information share, $P_g - b_g$, splits exactly into contributions of the encoded amplitudes, shown as Born evidence maps (BEM) over the picture. The split itself follows from known results on quadratic forms: with the transmitted light held fixed, it is what Integrated Gradients from a zero baseline and the Shapley value give. What we add is a way to measure it on the hardware that classifies, from class probabilities on a quantum chip or from camera frames on a lens bench, with no gradient circuit and no light sent backwards; a $g\times g$ map takes $1 + 2g^2$ runs. Deleting the 5% of pixels with the highest evidence drops accuracy from 73% to 9%, as occlusion does with 1,024 extra runs per picture, whereas gradient saliency removes much less. The classifiers share one architecture, a Fourier-plane mask followed by a brickwall circuit on qubits or by phase plates on a lens bench, read by a fixed Born headroom readout with no trained parameter; centring each picture on its own mean lets dark features count as much as bright ones. In simulation, four phase plates at a single wavelength reach 72.3% on Caltech-10 colour photographs. On IBM's ibm_kingston, with the mask applied before approximate loading, 300 test pictures were classified at 37.7% against 10% by chance (56.3% in exact simulation), and $2\times2$ maps of ten correctly classified pictures, one per class chosen by a stated rule, measured on the chip, agreed with the exact ones ($r = 0.77$). The maps also revealed a shortcut in the data; as the trim that removed it was chosen on test pictures, the Caltech-10 results are exploratory.
item.dc:creator: Teerawat Tongloy, Rangsan Jomtarak

item.title: GatedV: Self-Gated Values for Transformer Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.02145v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Standard attention forms query (Q), key (K), and value (V) matrices through learned linear projections of input hidden states. Architectures such as GAU and Mega incorporate nonlinear transformations into attention. In this paper, we propose GatedV, a simple attention variant that applies SiLU only to V before aggregation without introducing additional trainable parameters. We evaluate GatedV against a standard decoder-only Transformer using matched parameter counts, paired initializations, and equal training-token budgets. At 2.33M parameters, GatedV reduces mean held-out perplexity from 59.1 to 57.9 (2.0%), with improvements across all five paired seeds. At 26.16M parameters, following an equal-budget learning-rate search, mean held-out perplexity falls from 20.2 to 19.7 (2.4%), with improvements across all three paired seeds. Small-model ablations show that the tested affine rescaling of values does not fully reproduce GatedV's gains. A short interleaved benchmark on NVIDIA DGX Spark measures approximately 0.7% higher full-context forward latency for the larger model, based on synchronized wall-clock timings. These findings suggest that value-only self-gating can improve language modeling performance without increasing parameter count or redesigning the attention-weighting mechanism.
item.dc:creator: Li-Ming Yu, Hongyu Zhou

item.title: CR-Bench-v2: Evaluating the Real-World Utility of AI Code Review Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.02566v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rapid growth of automated code generation has created a pressing need for automated code review. Yet code review resists full automation: it depends on context beyond the \textit{diff}, on the author's intent, and on judgments about design and maintainability on which even expert reviewers disagree. Existing code review benchmarks lack standardization and rely largely on noisy human review comments scored with text-similarity metrics, which reward surface overlap and fail to measure precision. We introduce \texttt{CR-Bench}, a defect-centric evaluation framework that recasts SWE-Bench issues as pull-request review tasks with full repository context. After filtering for review-detectable defects and grounding each to a single originating pull request, \texttt{CR-Bench} contains 584 instances, with a 174-instance \texttt{CR-Bench-Verified} subset derived from SWE-Bench Verified. Each instance pairs a pull request with a known defect, its ground-truth fix, and a taxonomy label for bug category, impact, and severity. We propose two complementary metrics: \emph{Known-Defect Detection Rate} (KDDR), which measures whether an agent identifies the labeled defect, and \emph{Usefulness Rate}, which measures the fraction of review comments that are actionable. We evaluate eight code review agents over four backbones, plus commercially available Gemini Code Assist, using three independent LLM judges. Even the strongest systems detect only about one-third of known defects (KDDR $\approx$ 33\%), and Gemini Code Assist detects 8.1\%.
item.dc:creator: Kristen Pereira, Neelabh Sinha, Rajat Ghosh, Debojyoti Dutta

item.title: Why Tabular Foundation Models Excel on Relational Data They Have Never Seen
item.description: arXiv:2611.02936v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Given a relational database (RDB) storing heterogeneous tabular information, how can we predict missing (or future) values in some target column of interest? As candidate targets are numerous in enterprise settings, it is preferable to avoid learning a new model from scratch each time there is a new prediction task. Frozen foundation models (FMs) based on in-context learning (ICL) and RDB-specific pre-training provide a viable solution, but the ideal design still remains largely unresolved. Perhaps unexpectedly, preliminary evidence has recently shown that existing single-table FMs (aka TFMs), when combined with suitable parameter-free relational encoders, can be quite competitive in practice despite zero exposure to RDB pre-training or relational data of any kind. In this work we first empirically confirm this phenomenon with a more diverse array of experiments. We then turn to our main contribution, namely, surfacing multiple complementary explanations for why TFMs behave so effectively. These explanations ultimately hinge on innate synergies whereby parameter-free encoders map relational effects to fixed-length embeddings that loosely mimic distributions for which TFMs were originally designed; in so doing, desirable single-table properties transfer to relational settings (e.g., convergent posterior predictive distributions). Collectively, our analysis forges new pathways for improving RDB FMs, particularly when we prioritize interpretability and inevitable integration within agentic systems.
item.dc:creator: Linjie Xu, Yiqun Hu, Jixiang He, David Wipf
